idiom_name: Thread::Queue / Thread::SizedQueue (C implementation, mutex + condition variable)
implementation_notes: Ruby's core exposes no compare-and-swap: concurrent-ruby builds its atomic reference on a native extension on CRuby and falls back to MutexAtomicReference without it, and on JRuby/TruffleRuby it delegates to the VM's atomic class, so a pure-Ruby lock-free queue is a mutex in disguise. The standard hand-off is Thread::Queue, whose documentation states it implements all the required locking semantics in C, with SizedQueue adding bounded backpressure; the blocking pop is exactly what a consumer needs and what a CAS ring cannot provide without a parking protocol of its own. On CRuby the GVL further serialises bytecode, so lock-freedom buys no CPU parallelism - use Ractors or processes when parallel work is the goal.
alternative: Thread::Queue / Thread::SizedQueue (C-implemented, lock-based, blocking pop) for thread hand-off; concurrent-ruby for higher-level concurrency, or processes/Ractors for real parallelism.
code_sketch:
q = Thread::Queue.new
Thread.new { 5.times { |i| q << i } }        # producer
5.times { work(q.pop) }                      # consumer: blocks until an item arrives
# bounded: SizedQueue.new(4) - push blocks when full, giving backpressure
pitfalls: concurrent-ruby's atomics are mutex-backed without the native extension, so assuming they are lock-free silently reproduces the contention you meant to remove.
pop blocks, but an unbounded Queue with a faster producer still grows without limit - use SizedQueue when overload must be visible.
Thread::Queue is per-process: it does not share work across forked workers or Ractors, so multi-process pipelines need another channel.
